title: Qadar
def: God’s knowledge and decree of all things, held together with human responsibility for choices.
what: “Indeed, We created all things by measure” (54:49). The Prophet taught that belief in qadar, its good and its bad, is a pillar of faith (Sahih Muslim). Yet the Quran holds each soul responsible: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it” (99:7). Scholars teach that God’s knowledge does not force anyone’s choices.
sources: Early thinkers divided over it: the Qadariyya stressed human freedom, and the Jabriyya compulsion. Al-Ash‘ari and al-Maturidi each worked out a middle position.

title: Qarun
def: A man of Moses’ people whom the Quran gives as the example of wealth that leads to arrogance.
what: “Qarun was of the people of Moses, but he oppressed them. We gave him such treasures that the keys alone weighed down a band of strong men” (28:76). His people told him, “Do not exult; God does not love the exultant,” but he claimed his wealth by his own knowledge, and God caused the earth to swallow him (28:78–81).
sources: The Bible calls him Korah (Numbers 16), where the story differs in detail (rebellion against Moses’ leadership). The Quran takes the story for its own lesson, wealth as a test.

title: Qira’at
def: The recognised modes of reciting the Quran, taught by an unbroken chain of teachers.
what: Ten readings are recognised as authentic, each traced through a named teacher back to the Prophet. They share the same written skeleton and differ mostly in vowelling and pronunciation. Two are common today: Hafs, from Asim, in most of the Muslim world, and Warsh, from Nafi, in North and West Africa.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari relates that the Quran was “sent down in seven aḥruf”: Umar objected to how Hisham ibn Hakim was reciting, and the Prophet approved both recitations.
misread: That there are different Qurans, or that the text is unstable.
sources: The readings are variants within one text, and the great majority make no difference to the meaning. A few change a word in a way that adds a shade of meaning, and scholars treat these as additions to understanding rather than contradictions. The same standard text, in Hafs or Warsh, is in every mosque.

title: Qisas
def: The law of equal retribution for killing and injury, with the strong encouragement to forgive or accept compensation.
what: “O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you in the case of the killed” (2:178), followed by the words, “but whoever is forgiven by his brother, then let him follow it with fairness.” In the case of killing, the family of the victim may demand retribution, accept blood-money, or forgive for the sake of God (5:45, 42:40). Courts and proof are required.

title: Qiyas
def: Analogical reasoning, by which a ruling in the sources is applied to a new case sharing the same cause.
what: Jurists apply a ruling to a new matter when the reason for the ruling is present there too, for example the ban on wine extended to other intoxicants. It is the fourth source of law for most Sunni schools after the Quran, the Sunna and consensus. The report of Mu‘adh ibn Jabal, who said he would use his own reasoning when sources were silent, is cited as support, although its chain is discussed.

title: Quran
def: The recited scripture of Islam, revealed to Muhammad and kept in memory and in writing.
what: “Quran” means “recitation”. It has 114 chapters (suras) and is recited in Arabic in prayer. Its first revelation was the command “Read” (96:1). Muslims believe it is God’s word, preserved: “We have sent down the Reminder, and We will guard it” (15:9).

From the beginning it was kept in two ways at once: memorised by the community and written down. Under Abu Bakr the written leaves were gathered in one place, and under Uthman standard copies were prepared and sent to the main cities.
misread: That the Quran was edited, lost in part or rewritten by Uthman.
sources: Reports of the collection are in Sahih al-Bukhari, which names Zayd ibn Thabit as the scribe. On the manuscripts, a Quran leaf in the University of Birmingham’s collection was radiocarbon dated to between 568 and 645 CE, with a probability of 95.4 per cent, which is within or very near the Prophet’s lifetime. Muslims also point to the unbroken chain of recitation, taught from teacher to student to this day.

title: Quraysh
def: The leading tribe of Mecca, guardians of the Kaaba and the tribe of the Prophet.
what: The Quran has a surah named for them, which reminds them of the security of their trade caravans and bids them “worship the Lord of this House” (106:1–4). The Prophet belonged to the clan of Hashim. Most Quraysh opposed him for years and many entered Islam after the conquest of Mecca in 630.

title: Qurayza
def: A Jewish tribe of Medina whose siege and judgement in 627 followed their breach of the pact during the Battle of the Trench.
what: In the siege of the Trench the Banu Qurayza were accused of conspiring with the besieging army against Medina. After the siege, they surrendered and requested that Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh, their former ally, judge them. Sa‘d ruled by the law of the Torah, and the men who had fought were put to death (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: Historians dispute the number executed, and some modern scholars question details of the account. The Quran refers to the event at 33:26–27. Muslim scholars stress that it was a judgement on treason in wartime, not on a people for their faith.

title: Qaddara
def: To measure, assign and bring about according to plan; also to be able to make something happen.
what: Qaddara means to measure out, to assign a thing its measure and to bring it about according to a plan. It also carries the sense of having the power to make something happen. The Quran uses it of God, who created everything and ordained it in due measure (25:2), and states that He created all things by measure (54:49). From this root come qadar, the measure or decree that God has set, and qudrah, power, together with the divine name al-Qadīr, the All-Powerful. Muslim teaching on qadar holds that nothing happens outside God’s knowledge and ordering, while a person remains responsible for choices and conduct.
misread: That it means blind fate, when it points to a plan made by a knowing and powerful Lord.

title: Qasas
def: The reports and narratives of those who relate, as in qaṣṣa; in the Quran, accounts of earlier peoples.
what: Qaṣaṣ is the plural noun for accounts that are related, formed from the verb qaṣṣa, to relate. It is the word for the stories and reports narrated, above all those of earlier prophets and peoples that the Quran tells in order to teach. The Quran speaks of itself as the best of narratives (12:3), and a whole chapter, al-Qaṣaṣ (chapter 28), takes its name from the word. Muslims read these accounts as lessons and warnings, set down with a purpose, and not as entertainment.
misread: That the Quranic stories are legends or folktales, when the term means true reports told for guidance.

title: Qassa
def: To relate reports or matters about earlier times, especially about earlier prophets.
what: Qaṣṣa is an Arabic verb meaning to relate, to tell a report or a matter, particularly one from earlier times. It is used of the telling of the stories of earlier prophets and peoples, and the Quran uses it of God Himself, who relates the best of narratives to Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the Quran (12:3). The related noun qaṣaṣ names the reports that are related. The root also gives qiṣṣah, a story, and the Quran adds that in the accounts of the earlier prophets there is a lesson for people of understanding (12:111).
misread: That the telling of prophetic history is idle story, when the verb carries a truthful reporting of the past.

title: Qiblah
def: The direction of Makkah al-Mukarramah, which Muslims face in salah.
what: The qiblah is the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah al-Mukarramah, which Muslims face when they perform the salah. It is also the direction in which a Muslim is laid in the grave. A mosque is built so that its prayer niche (miḥrāb) marks it. In the first years after the migration to Madinah, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the believers faced Jerusalem. The Quran then directed him to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque, and the believers with him (2:144). Muslims everywhere, wherever they are on earth, turn toward that one point, which gives the community a shared centre in worship.
misread: That Muslims worship the Kaaba, when it is only the direction they face in worshipping God alone.

title: Qisas, al-
def: The retributive and compensatory punishment prescribed for homicide and for injury to a person.
what: Al-Qiṣāṣ is the law of equal retribution for killing and for bodily injury. It allows the victim or the family of the victim to demand a penalty equal to the harm done, and it also allows them to forgive the offender or to accept compensation instead. The compensation for a life or an injury is called diya. The Quran prescribes it for the killed (2:178) and says that in qiṣāṣ there is life for people of understanding (2:179). It also lists the principle of a life for a life and like for like in wounds, and calls forgiveness an act of charity that wipes away sins for the one who forgives (5:45).
misread: That it is only vengeance, when it limits the response to the harm done and invites forgiveness.
sources: The jurists treat qiṣāṣ as a right of the injured party, and the state carries out the judgment after the court has proved the case. The Quran puts forgiveness above retribution, and a judge may not impose it where the family has pardoned.

title: Qist
def: Justice, equity and uprightness in all dealings; the verbal noun of aqsaṭa.
what: Qisṭ means justice, equity and uprightness in dealing with all matters. It is the verbal noun of the verb aqsaṭa, to act justly, and the one who acts justly is the muqsiṭ. It stresses even-handed fairness in weight, judgment and treatment of others. The Quran commands believers to stand firmly for justice (qisṭ), as witnesses for God, even against themselves or their kin (4:135; see also 5:8). It says that God loves the just (al-muqsiṭīn) (49:9), and that He sent His messengers with the Book and the balance so that people may uphold justice (57:25).
misread: That it is only a legal term, when the Quran treats it as a standing duty in every dealing.

title: Qiyas, al-
def: Reasoning by analogy from the Quran and the Sunnah, as a source of Islamic law.
what: Al-Qiyās is logical deduction applied to the sources of Islamic law. When no text of the Quran or of the Sunnah, nor consensus (ijmāʿ), settles a new case, the jurist compares it with a case that a text does settle, finds the shared reason (ʿillah), and extends the ruling to the new case. Most Sunni jurists count it as the fourth source of law, after the Quran, the Sunnah and consensus, and the schools differ on how widely they apply it. It is the main means by which the law meets circumstances the early community did not face.
misread: That jurists invent law from opinion, when qiyās works from a stated reason found in the sources.

title: Qur'an Al-Karim, al-
def: God’s final revelation to Muhammad (peace be upon him), given in Arabic, memorized and recited from the start, and written in its present form by order of Uthman.
what: Al-Qurʾān al-Karīm, the Noble Quran, is the final revelation of God’s will, given in Arabic to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). His Companions memorized it word for word and recited it publicly and continuously, as their descendants have done to the present day. Its present written form was prepared by order of Uthman ibn Affan (may God be pleased with him), the third of the Rashidun caliphs, in about 24-25 A.H. (646-647 C.E.). The Quran states that God sent down the reminder and will guard it (15:9). Muslims treat the Arabic text as the Quran itself, and a translation as an interpretation of its meanings.
misread: That the Quran is the Prophet’s own writing or a translated book, when Muslims hold its wording to be from God.

title: Qu'ud
def: The act of sitting during the salah.
what: Quʿūd is sitting in the salah. It is one of the postures of the prayer, along with standing (qiyām), bowing (rukūʿ) and prostration (sujūd). The worshipper sits after the prostrations, and sits again at the end of the unit of prayer to recite the tashahhud and invoke blessings on the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The sitting takes the place of standing for a person who cannot stand. The Quran praises those who remember God standing, sitting and lying on their sides (3:191). Sitting is a part of the structure that the Prophet taught and that Muslims follow in every prayer.
misread: That any rest during prayer is optional, when sitting is a set part of the prayer.
